# Accuracy at full data, and robustness {#sec-full-data}

**At full DrivAerML data and the reporting protocol, ISLA and GeoTransolver
are at parity and ISLA leads Transolver by 6%; off the tuned operating
point, ISLA is the configuration that survives.** With every model fed the
same inputs, each at its own best learning rate, and scored in float32 at
200,000 cells per case, GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA is 0.998 and Transolver ÷ ISLA
1.06 (@sec-scoreboard-200k); the gap the baselines hold at smaller cell
budgets is count noise (@sec-deficit-anatomy). What separates the
architectures is what happens when the evaluation departs from the training
conditions. Under a 10:1 sampling-density bias at inference ISLA's error
grows 1.07x at 100,000 cells where GeoTransolver's grows 8.7x and
Transolver's 5.3x; trained under a different sampling law and scored on
the usual one, GeoTransolver and Transolver are 2.4 to 2.6x worse on the
wings and 7.9 to 9.6x worse on the cars while ISLA moves 1% and 8%, weakly
dependent beside baselines that are dependent by factors; under refinement
ISLA converges toward one answer while the baselines do not; in arbitrary
poses ISLA's exact covariance is worth 12% and 21% against
rotation-augmented baselines at the reporting protocol; and it trains at
its protocol learning rate without a sweep, though under linear routing
inside a rate ceiling that falls with width and depth, which cosine routing
removes (@sec-robustness-lr). Both architectures reach the same accuracy
floor of about 0.040 on the cars, GeoTransolver along width and ISLA along
depth at half the parameters (@sec-shared-floor). Across a flow-regime
boundary nothing tested generalizes.

The metric everywhere is the area-weighted relative L2 of surface pressure
in float32 (@sec-metrics), and a ratio is baseline ÷ ISLA, above one
favoring ISLA. Every ISLA number in this chapter is ISLA unless labeled
otherwise; the legacy centered variant (removed from the class;
@sec-isla-variants) appears only in the regime-extrapolation table, where
it stands in for ISLA and is labeled "removed variant". Each section states its cell budget
in its first lines: the reporting protocol is 200,000 cells per case, the
exploration budget 10,000, and the scaling budget 100,000 (cells are flat
above 100,000 for every model, @sec-equal-budget). The scoreboard
(@sec-scoreboard) has every DrivAerML row with seeds and artifacts; this
chapter explains what stands behind the rows.

```{python}
#| include: false

from pathlib import Path
RES = Path("..") / "results"
```

## Learning-rate robustness {#sec-robustness-lr}

**ISLA trains at its protocol rate of 1e-3 without a sweep, and under
linear routing that rate is a ceiling: the highest clean rate falls like
1/width and at least as fast as 1/depth, and above it training fails
totally, every point routing to one slice and every anchor coincident.
Cosine routing removes the ceiling on every DrivAerML lane tested at
neutral accuracy; the wing lanes decide the default.**
Budget: the width-192 window below was measured at the exploration budget
of 10,000 cells; the width and depth ladders at the scaling budget of
100,000. At width 192 and 3e-3 both seeds settle within five epochs on a
mean-field plateau (validation loss 0.06 against 0.0008 at 1e-3; float32
pressure error 0.77 against 0.055) and never leave it; at 1e-2 the loss is
NaN by epoch 21 and 32 (@sec-nb-lrref-verdict). The window was bracketed
(@sec-nb-ratewindow-verdict): 3e-4 scores 1.08x the 1e-3 error (the same
curve, undertrained in 500 epochs) and 2e-3 already rises to the plateau by
epoch 22, so the safe window at width 192 is 3e-4 to 1e-3. GeoTransolver
one grid step above its best rate degrades 9.0x on DrivAerML and 6.5x on
HiLiftAeroML by seed mean (full-split grids at the 10,000-cell exploration
budget, bfloat16; results/instrument_wave_reduction_2026-09-01.json,
results/highlift_wave_reduction.json) and its error stays an order of
magnitude below the mean-field value: a graded degradation, not a plateau.

```{python}

#| output: asis

RN = json.load(open(RES / "routenorm_interim_2026-09-20.json"))

EXT = json.load(open(RES / "routenorm_extension_2026-09-21.json"))["configurations"]

acc = RNB["accuracy_at_rule_rates"]
print(f"The plateau is total routing collapse, measured on the plateau lanes themselves: every point routes to one slice in every "
      "block and the anchors coincide, after which the model sees no geometry, while clean checkpoints keep 4 to 250 active slices "
      f"per block (@sec-nb-routingsat-verdict). The ceiling scales. At 384 wide the rule rate 5e-4 trains cleanly ({lin('isla|w384|d12|s256|lr5e-4'):.4f}) "
      f"and 1e-3 sits on the plateau ({lin('isla|w384|d12|s256|lr1e-3'):.2f}); at 768 wide 2.5e-4 is clean ({lin('isla|w768|d12|s256|lr2.5e-4'):.4f}) "
```

## The sampling laws in one picture {#sec-sampling-laws}

**Every discretization result in this chapter is a statement about which
cells of a surface mesh a model gets to see, and with what weight; four
draws recur, and @fig-sampling-laws shows all four on one meshed
section.** A surface arrives as a mesh whose cells the mesher has refined
where it expected gradients (leading and trailing edges here, the
A-pillars and mirrors of a car in DrivAerML). A training or evaluation
sample keeps a subset of $n$ of the $N$ cells; each kept cell $i$ carries
its Horvitz–Thompson weight $1/\pi_i$, the reciprocal of its inclusion
probability, so that any cell-weighted sum over the kept cells estimates
the same surface integral without bias whatever the draw. The four draws
differ only in $\pi_i$:

- **Uniform over cells** (the training convention of every model in this
  book): every cell kept with probability $n/N$, every weight $N/n$. The
  kept points inherit the mesher's refinement, so the model sees a point
  cloud that is dense exactly where the mesher was.
- **Stratified** (the same law, lower variance): one cell per consecutive
  run of $N/n$ cells along the Morton (Z-order) curve through the cell
  centroids, with one random offset. Same inclusion probability and
  weights as the uniform draw, but no two kept cells are neighbours and
  no run is skipped, so slice integrals have less draw-to-draw noise.
- **10:1 front/back bias** (the density-bias probe): cells with centroid
  $x$ ahead of the per-sample median draw with ten times the probability
  of the rest, kept independently (Poisson sampling) with exact $\pi_i$.
  The front of the body is over-sampled and each rear cell that is kept
  stands for about ten times more surface than a front one.
- **Area-proportional** (the law a uniform point generator over the
  *surface* would produce): $\pi_i$ proportional to the cell's area, so
  the kept points are spread evenly over the surface regardless of the
  mesher's refinement; a large cell is nearly always kept and carries a
  small weight, a tiny leading-edge cell is rarely kept and carries a
  large one.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sampling-laws
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The four draws on one meshed section (a Joukowski airfoil at 6° with
#|   a mesher-like refinement at the leading and trailing edges, 400 cells;
#|   the small ticks mark the cell boundaries). Top four panels: the cells
#|   kept by each draw at an expected 80 of 400, one marker per kept cell
#|   with marker area proportional to its Horvitz–Thompson weight (how much
#|   surface it stands for). Bottom: the density of kept points along the
#|   surface for each draw, against the mesh's own cell density (gray) and
#|   the uniform-over-the-surface level (dashed). The uniform and stratified
#|   draws follow the mesh's refinement; the 10:1 bias piles points onto the
#|   front half; the area-proportional draw is flat over the surface, with
#|   the mesher's refinement moved entirely into the weights. How to read
#|   this: the draws are computed with the recipe's own inclusion rules
#|   (PoissonBiasedSubsampleMesh, StratifiedSubsampleMesh); the section and
#|   its mesh are an illustration, not a dataset surface. Weights span 1 to
#|   10 under the bias and 1 to 10 under the area law here; on the
#|   DrivAerML and HiLiftAeroML meshes the area-law weights span four
#|   decades.
#| code-fold: true
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
N, n = 400, 80
s_fine = np.linspace(0, 1, 20001)
rho = 1 + 9 * np.exp(-((s_fine - 0.5) / 0.05) ** 2) + 5 * np.exp(-(s_fine / 0.035) ** 2) + 5 * np.exp(-((s_fine - 1) / 0.035) ** 2)
cdf = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(rho[1:] * np.diff(s_fine))]); cdf /= cdf[-1]
Jm = joukowski(alpha_deg=6.0, n_cells=N, frac=np.interp(np.linspace(0, 1, N + 1), cdf, s_fine))
xy, mid, w = Jm["xy"], Jm["mid"], Jm["w"]  # w = cell length, the 1-D measure
s_mid = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(w)])[:-1] + w / 2; s_mid /= w.sum()
def uniform_draw():
    return np.sort(rng.choice(N, n, replace=False)), np.full(N, n / N)
def stratified_draw():  # Morton (Z-order) systematic sample, as StratifiedSubsampleMesh
    lo = mid.min(axis=0); span = mid.max(axis=0) - lo; q = np.round((mid - lo) / span * (2**16 - 1)).astype(np.int64)
    code = np.zeros(N, dtype=np.int64)
    for b in range(16):
        for ax_ in range(2):
            code |= ((q[:, ax_] >> b) & 1) << (2 * b + ax_)
    order = np.argsort(code); step = N / n; off = rng.random() * step
    return np.sort(order[np.floor(off + step * np.arange(n)).astype(int).clip(max=N - 1)]), np.full(N, n / N)
def poisson_draw(wts):  # independent sampling with exact pi, as PoissonBiasedSubsampleMesh
    c = n / wts.sum(); pi = np.minimum(1.0, c * wts); deficit = n - pi.sum()
    if deficit > 0:
        free = pi < 1; pi[free] = np.minimum(1.0, pi[free] * (1 + deficit / pi[free].sum()))
    return np.nonzero(rng.random(N) < pi)[0], pi
x_med = np.median(mid[:, 0])
LAWS = [("uniform over cells", INK2, uniform_draw), ("stratified (Morton systematic)", VIOLET, stratified_draw),
        ("10:1 front/back bias", "#b5179e", lambda: poisson_draw(np.where(mid[:, 0] < x_med, 10.0, 1.0))),
        ("area-proportional", GREEN, lambda: poisson_draw(w.copy()))]
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(10.2, 7.4))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(3, 2, height_ratios=[0.62, 0.62, 1.0], hspace=0.35, wspace=0.04)
axes = [fig.add_subplot(gs[i // 2, i % 2]) for i in range(4)]
densities = []
for ax, (name, col, draw) in zip(axes, LAWS):
    idx, pi = draw(); ht = 1.0 / pi[idx]
    ax.plot(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], color=BASELINE, lw=1.0, zorder=1)
    nb = Jm["nrm"]
    for k in range(N):
        p = xy[k]; d = nb[k]
        ax.plot([p[0], p[0] + 0.05 * d[0]], [p[1], p[1] + 0.05 * d[1]], color=MUTED, lw=0.5, zorder=0)
    ax.scatter(mid[idx, 0], mid[idx, 1], s=9.0 * ht, c=col, alpha=0.85, zorder=3, lw=0)
    clean_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.3, 2.3); ax.set_ylim(-0.55, 0.62)
    ax.set_title(name, color=col, fontsize=10)
    ax.text(0.5, -0.02, f"{len(idx)} of {N} cells kept; weights 1/π from {ht.min():.1f} to {ht.max():.1f}", transform=ax.transAxes,
            fontsize=8.5, color=INK2, va="top", ha="center", path_effects=halo())
    if name.startswith("10:1"):
        ax.axvline(x_med, color=col, lw=0.8, ls=":", zorder=2); ax.text(x_med + 0.05, 0.5, "median x: 10:1 weight to the left", color=col, fontsize=8, ha="left", va="center")
    grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 200); bw = 0.02
    densities.append((name, col, np.array([np.sum(np.exp(-0.5 * ((g - s_mid[idx]) / bw) ** 2)) for g in grid]) / (bw * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi)) / w.sum()))
axd = fig.add_subplot(gs[2, :]); grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)
mesh_dens = np.interp(grid, s_mid, 1 / (w / w.sum()) / N)
axd.fill_between(grid, 0, mesh_dens / mesh_dens.mean() * (n / w.sum()), color=GRID, zorder=0, label="the mesh itself: cells per unit length, scaled to n")
for name, col, dens in densities:
    axd.plot(grid, dens, color=col, lw=1.8, zorder=3, label=name)
axd.axhline(n / w.sum(), color=INK2, lw=0.8, ls="--", zorder=2)
axd.text(0.995, n / w.sum(), "uniform over the surface (n ÷ perimeter)", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=8, color=INK2, transform=axd.get_yaxis_transform(), path_effects=halo())
for s_, lab in ((0.0, "trailing edge"), (0.5, "leading edge"), (1.0, "trailing edge")):
    axd.axvline(s_, color=BASELINE, lw=0.8); axd.text(s_, 1.5, lab, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8, color=MUTED, path_effects=halo())
axd.set_xlabel("position along the surface [fraction of arclength, lower surface → leading edge → upper surface]")
axd.set_ylabel("kept points per\nunit surface length [1/chord]")
axd.set_xlim(0, 1); axd.set_ylim(0, 75); axd.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8.5)
plt.show()
```

Two of these draws also serve as *training* laws. Every model in the book
is trained under the uniform-over-cells law unless a section says
otherwise; @sec-training-law trains each model a second time under the
area-proportional law and scores both under the same independent uniform
draw, which is how the dependence of a trained function on the sampling
law it saw is measured. The measure weights are what make the swap fair:
a model that aggregates with them sees the same integrals under all four
draws; a model that averages the kept points as if they were equally
representative sees four different point clouds.

## Sampling-density robustness {#sec-robustness-density}

**Under a 10:1 spatially biased sampling density at inference ISLA's error
grows 1.07x at 100,000 cells; GeoTransolver's and Transolver's, which
center their coordinates on the sampled points, grow 8.7x and 5.3x.**
Budget: the scaling budget of 100,000 cells; the factors come from the
uniform-trained arms of the training-law study (@sec-training-law). The
probe evaluates a trained DrivAerML
model on the 48 validation cars with surface points drawn ten times more
densely at the front of the car than at the back (the third panel of
@fig-sampling-laws), with exact Horvitz–Thompson measure weights so that
every weighted integral is unbiased; the readout is the error under the biased draw divided by the
same model's error under uniform sampling at the same count. A ratio of 1
means the prediction depends only on the surface and not on how it was
sampled. Every ratio states its frame: the *sample frame* centers each
model's coordinates on the biased sample itself, which is what a biased
mesher delivers and what ISLA computes inside the model; the *pool frame*
hands a model an unbiased center it would not have in deployment and
appears only where it is the value on file.

The mechanism is the one taught in @sec-isla-frame. ISLA has no origin: translation invariance comes from
point-to-anchor differences, and its length unit is an integral of the
sampled surface that the biased draw estimates without bias (the lanes
quoted in the table carry the total-measure unit; the default
RMS-pairwise-distance unit is also a measure-weighted integral of the
surface). GeoTransolver
and Transolver consume coordinates centered by the datapipe on the plain
mean of the sampled points, which moves by 0.94 RMS radii under the 10:1
bias, and every downstream quantity moves with it.

```{python}
#| label: para-density-100k
#| output: asis
TDR = json.load(open(RES / "trainarea_dr_reduction_2026-09-20.json"))["arms"]
bf = lambda m: TDR[f"{m}_uniform"]["mean"]["biased"] / TDR[f"{m}_uniform"]["mean"]["unif"]
print(f"At the scaling budget of 100,000 cells per case (435 cars, uniform-trained checkpoints, float32, two seeds) the same 10:1 bias "
      f"multiplies the surface-pressure error by {bf('isla'):.2f}x for ISLA, {bf('gt_unit'):.1f}x for GeoTransolver and {bf('transolver_unit'):.1f}x "
      "for Transolver, sample frame; the stratified draw is within 2% of the uniform one for every model. More cells shrink ISLA's "
      "residual, which is the variance of its measure-weighted routing integral, and do not shrink the baselines' factor, which is the frame. "
      "Data: results/trainarea_dr_reduction_2026-09-20.json (uniform-trained arms, biased ÷ uniform).")
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-density
#| output: asis
out = "| configuration | uniform 100,000-cell error | biased ÷ uniform, sample frame |\n|---|---:|---:|\n"
for lab, m in (("ISLA", "isla"), ("GeoTransolver", "gt_unit"), ("Transolver", "transolver_unit")):
    u = TDR[f"{m}_uniform"]["mean"]
    out += f"| {lab} | {u['unif']:.4f} | {u['biased']/u['unif']:.2f}x |\n"
print(out)
print(": Sampling-density robustness on DrivAerML at the scaling budget of 100,000 cells, float32, 48 validation cars, uniform-trained checkpoints of the training-law study, each architecture at its reporting-protocol rate: surface-pressure error under uniform "
      "sampling, and the same checkpoint's error under 10:1 biased inclusion with exact Horvitz–Thompson weights divided by its "
      "uniform error, input frame from the biased sample (seed means; 1.0 means sampling-independent predictions). How to read this: the three released "
      "models are the comparison at one bias pattern and one count; it does not show the ablations that locate the sensitivity (below) or any other dataset. "
      "Data: results/trainarea_dr_reduction_2026-09-20.json. {#tbl-density}")
```

Two things follow. The sensitivity is the **frame, not the aggregation**:
in the ablations GeoTransolver + ISLA's measure-weighted pooling keeps the
baselines' factor where it was, and GeoTransolver + ISLA's measure-weighted
pooling + Horvitz–Thompson-centered datapipe brings it close to one
(@sec-nb-steelman-verdict; @tbl-consistency-40k below carries the
pooling ablation). ISLA's residual, 1.07x at 100,000 cells and larger at
smaller counts, is the **variance of its measure-weighted routing
integral** under a 10:1 sample, not a frame effect. The scope is one bias
pattern at one ratio on one dataset; the benchmark below varies the
sampling law and the count.

## Consistency under refinement and across samplers {#sec-consistency-bench}

**No configuration gives the same field under a different sampling of the
same surface at 10,000 cells; ISLA's relative frame converges toward it as
the sample grows, and GeoTransolver and Transolver do not.** Budget: the
checkpoints are the exploration-budget lanes (trained at 10,000 cells; the
ISLA lanes carry the total-measure length unit), evaluated at 2,500 to
40,000 cells.
The consistency benchmark asks the question the principle of @sec-principle
poses: does a model converge to one field under refinement, and to the same
field under two sampling laws? Every checkpoint was evaluated in float32 on
the same validation surfaces sampled three ways from a 320,000-cell pool at
2,500 to 40,000 cells: uniformly over cells (the training convention, which
inherits the mesher's refinement), proportionally to cell area (the law a
uniform point-cloud generator would produce), and with the 10:1 bias; each
draw carries exact Horvitz–Thompson weights, so a measure-consistent model
sees the same integral under all three.

```{python}
#| label: fig-consistency-curves
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Convergence toward consistency. Each panel plots an architecture's
#|   surface-pressure error divided by the same architecture's error under
#|   uniform sampling at 40,000 cells, against the number of sampled cells,
#|   for three samplers (columns) and two validation sets (rows); a curve
#|   approaching 1 converges to the uniform-sampling answer. Uniform sampling
#|   (left) converges for every arm. Under the area-proportional sampler
#|   (middle) the ISLA arms fall toward 1 while the baselines are
#|   flat. Under the 10:1 bias (right) the ISLA arms approach the uniform
#|   answer at 40,000 cells. ISLA was benchmarked from
#|   10,000 cells, so its curves start there. How to read this: only the
#|   trend with count is interpretable under the area sampler, whose weights
#|   span four decades and leave refined regions unsampled at small counts,
#|   so fixed-count values there mix information loss with model dependence.
#|   Seed means over two seeds; float32; each checkpoint under its training
#|   snapshot. Data: results/consistency_bench/consistency_bench_2026-09-10.json,
#|   results/consistency_bench/consistency_bench_rf_2026-09-11.json.
#| code-fold: true
B = json.load(open(RES / "consistency_bench" / "consistency_bench_2026-09-10.json"))
A = dict(B["arms"]); COUNTS = [str(c) for c in B["counts"]]
A.update(json.load(open(RES / "consistency_bench" / "consistency_bench_rf_2026-09-11.json"))["arms"])
ROWS = [
 ("DrivAerML, 48 cars", {"isla_ref": "rf_dr_mt2_meas", "gt": "uw_gt_unit_lr1e3", "t": "uw_transolver_unit_lr3e3"}),
 ("HiLift, 35 training cases", {"isla_ref": "rf_hl_mt2_meas_super_scarce", "gt": "udrv_hl_gt_super_scarce_lr3e3", "t": "udrv_hl_transolver_super_scarce_lr3e3"}),
]
LABELS = {}
SAMPLERS = [("unif", "uniform over cells"), ("area", "area-proportional"), ("biased", "10:1 front/back bias")]
def err(arm, sampler, count):
    return A[arm]["table"][sampler][count]["pressure_l2"]["mean"]
fig, axs = plt.subplots(len(ROWS), 3, figsize=(10.2, 6.6), sharex=True)
x = [int(c) for c in COUNTS]
for i, (row_title, arms) in enumerate(ROWS):
    for j, (sampler, stitle) in enumerate(SAMPLERS):
        ax = axs[i, j]
        for key, arm in arms.items():
            counts = [c for c in COUNTS if c in A[arm]["table"][sampler]]
            ref = err(arm, "unif", "40000")
            y = [err(arm, sampler, c) / ref for c in counts]
            ax.plot([int(c) for c in counts], y, **series_kwargs(key, lw=1.6, ms=5, label=(LABELS.get(key, STYLE[key]["label"]) if (i == 0 and j == 0) else None)), zorder=3)
        ax.axhline(1.0, color=BASELINE, lw=1.0, zorder=1)
        ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
        ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mpl.ticker.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:g}")); ax.yaxis.set_minor_formatter(mpl.ticker.NullFormatter())
        ax.set_xticks(x); ax.set_xticklabels(["2.5k", "5k", "10k", "20k", "40k"]); ax.set_xlim(2100, 4.8e4)
        if i == 0: ax.set_title(stitle, fontsize=10)
        if j == 0: ax.set_ylabel(f"{row_title}\nerror ÷ own uniform-40k error [–]")
        if i == len(ROWS) - 1: ax.set_xlabel("sampled cells per case [count]")
handles, labels_ = axs[0, 0].get_legend_handles_labels()
fig.legend(handles, labels_, loc="upper left", ncol=4, fontsize=8.5, bbox_to_anchor=(0.01, 0.99), handlelength=2.4, columnspacing=1.4)
fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.93))
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-consistency-40k
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
for name in ("consistency_bench_mcenter_2026-09-10.json", "consistency_bench_mw_2026-09-10.json"):
    A.update(json.load(open(RES / "consistency_bench" / name))["arms"])
def D(arm, sampler, count="40000"):
    return A[arm]["D"][sampler][count]["pressure_l2"]
def conv(arm, sampler):
    t = A[arm]["table"][sampler]; lo = "2500" if "2500" in t else "10000"
    return t[lo]["pressure_l2"]["mean"] / t["40000"]["pressure_l2"]["mean"]
rows = [("DrivAerML", "ISLA", "rf_dr_mt2_meas"),
        ("DrivAerML", "GeoTransolver", "uw_gt_unit_lr1e3"), ("DrivAerML", "Transolver", "uw_transolver_unit_lr3e3"),
        ("DrivAerML", "GeoTransolver + ISLA's measure-weighted pooling (ablation; pool frame)", "mw_dr_gt_unit_lr1e3"), ("DrivAerML", "Transolver + ISLA's measure-weighted pooling (ablation; pool frame)", "mw_dr_transolver_unit_lr3e3"),
        ("HiLift 35", "ISLA", "rf_hl_mt2_meas_super_scarce"),
        ("HiLift 35", "GeoTransolver", "udrv_hl_gt_super_scarce_lr3e3"), ("HiLift 35", "Transolver", "udrv_hl_transolver_super_scarce_lr3e3"),
        ("HiLift 35", "GeoTransolver + ISLA's measure-weighted pooling (ablation; pool frame)", "mw_hl_gt_super_scarce_lr3e3"), ("HiLift 35", "Transolver + ISLA's measure-weighted pooling (ablation; pool frame)", "mw_hl_transolver_super_scarce_lr3e3")]
def table_rows(rows):
    out = "| validation set | configuration | uniform 40k error | area ÷ uniform − 1 at 40k | bias ÷ uniform − 1 at 40k | area-curve fall, first count → 40k |\n|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n"
    for ds, label, arm in rows:
        u40 = A[arm]["table"]["unif"]["40000"]["pressure_l2"]["mean"]
        out += f"| {ds} | {label} | {u40:.4f} | {D(arm,'area'):+.0%} | {D(arm,'biased'):+.1%} | {conv(arm,'area'):.2f}x |\n"
    return out
print(table_rows(rows))
print(": Consistency at the benchmark's largest count. The preregistered bars are a sampler dependence of at most 3% for consistent and at least 10% for reading the sampling distribution. ISLA passes both samplers on the wings at 35 cases and converges to within 3 to 4% on the cars; GeoTransolver and Transolver read the sampling distribution by 90% or more. The measure-weighted baselines' area and bias columns are pool-frame values: with the frame held, measure weighting makes their aggregation consistent; centered on the drawn sample their frame degrades by the same factors, and holds only when the center is the Horvitz–Thompson estimate of the geometric centroid (@sec-robustness-density). The last column is the factor by which each arm's area-sampler error fell over the counts it was run at (2,500 to 40,000 cells; 10,000 to 40,000 for ISLA). How to read this: the two middle columns are a model's distance from sampling independence at 40,000 cells, not an accuracy ranking; the checkpoints are exploration-budget lanes (trained at 10,000 cells), and the table shows neither the reporting-protocol checkpoints nor any count above 40,000. Float32, two-seed means. Data: results/consistency_bench/consistency_bench_2026-09-10.json and its _mw and _rf companions. {#tbl-consistency-40k}")
```

Three readings, in order of weight. **Consistency in the fine-mesh limit is
a property of the measure-weighted estimator standing on a frame that
reads no sample statistic.** ISLA has that frame by
construction and shows the property: on DrivAerML its area-sampler and bias
dependence fall from +41% and +19% at 10,000 cells to +3.4% and +2.5% at
40,000; on the 35-case HiLift rung it is within 1.3% and 0.9% at 40,000;
on the fixed-angle rung it converges to +2.6% and +5.5%, still short of the
bar there. **No configuration is consistent at the 10,000 cells of the
exploration budget**, and a factor-of-ten probe understates how far
each stands from consistency, since a different mesher changes the local
density by thousands. **On the wings, whose refinement spans more decades
than the cars', the sample-centered configurations do not converge within
40,000 cells**; their HiLift rows report the distance, not a verdict.

### Training under a different law: two datasets {#sec-training-law}

**A GeoTransolver or Transolver checkpoint is accurate on the sampling
law it was trained under and on no other: trained on the area-proportional
draw and scored on the uniform one it is 2.4 to 2.6x worse on the wings
and 7.9 to 9.6x worse on the cars, while ISLA moves 1% and 8%.** Budget:
200,000 cells per case on the wings (the reporting protocol), 100,000 on
the cars (the scaling budget; cells are flat above 100,000). Changing
the draw at inference (@tbl-consistency-40k) is one half of the
discretization question; changing the law the model was *trained* under is
the other, and it is the half a practitioner meets when a surrogate trained
on one mesher's output is handed a mesh from another. On each dataset the
three models were trained twice, under the uniform-over-cells law and under
the area-proportional Poisson law of @fig-sampling-laws with exact
Horvitz–Thompson weights, and every checkpoint was scored on the same
validation surfaces under the same independent uniform draw (float32, two
seeds; 35 wings at 200,000 cells, 435 cars at 100,000).

```{python}

    for k, (key, m) in enumerate((("isla_ref", "isla"), ("gt", "gt_unit"), ("t", "transolver_unit"))):
        u = arms[f"{m}_uniform"]["mean"]["unif"]; a = arms[f"{m}_area"]["mean"]["unif"]
        us = [arms[f"{m}_uniform"]["per_seed"][s]["unif"] for s in ("seed42", "seed43")]; as_ = [arms[f"{m}_area"]["per_seed"][s]["unif"] for s in ("seed42", "seed43")]
        kw = series_kwargs(key)
        ax.plot([k - 0.18, k + 0.18], [u, a], color=kw["color"], lw=1.6, zorder=2)
        ax.plot([k - 0.18], [u], marker=kw["marker"], color=kw["color"], mfc=kw["color"], mec=kw["color"], ls="none", ms=8, zorder=4)
        ax.plot([k + 0.18], [a], marker=kw["marker"], color=kw["color"], mfc="white", mec=kw["color"], mew=1.8, ls="none", ms=8, zorder=4)
        ax.plot([k - 0.18] * 2, us, ls="none", marker="o", color=kw["color"], ms=3.5, zorder=5); ax.plot([k + 0.18] * 2, as_, ls="none", marker="o", color=kw["color"], ms=3.5, zorder=5)
        ax.text(k + 0.24, a, f"×{a / u:.2f}" if a / u < 2 else f"×{a / u:.1f}", color=kw["color"], fontsize=9, va="center", path_effects=halo())
```

```{python}
      f"{C['gt_unit_area']['mean']['unif']/C['isla_area']['mean']['unif']:.1f}x and {C['transolver_unit_area']['mean']['unif']/C['isla_area']['mean']['unif']:.1f}x on the cars; under the uniform law it trails them by 27% on the wings and is at parity on the cars. "
      f"The same table carries the inference-side statement at 100,000 cells on the cars: the uniform-trained GeoTransolver and Transolver under the 10:1 biased draw are {C['gt_unit_uniform']['mean']['biased']/C['gt_unit_uniform']['mean']['unif']:.1f}x and "
      f"{C['transolver_unit_uniform']['mean']['biased']/C['transolver_unit_uniform']['mean']['unif']:.1f}x their uniform-draw error, ISLA {C['isla_uniform']['mean']['biased']/C['isla_uniform']['mean']['unif']:.2f}x.")
```

The mechanism is the one @sec-isla-quadrature teaches: the baselines' slice
aggregates are averages over the kept points, so the trained function
absorbs the point pattern it was fitted on and is wrong on any other;
ISLA's are measure-weighted integrals, the same under any draw that
carries its weights. @sec-territories looks at this directly in the two
trained networks. Two qualifications travel with the figure.
ISLA is not indifferent: 8% on the cars is past the 5% bar the
DrivAerML twin preregistered (@sec-nb-trainarea-dr-verdict), so the
statement is "weakly dependent" beside baselines that are dependent by
factors of 2.4 to 9.6; part of the 8% is the quadrature noise of an
area-proportional draw whose weights span four decades on these meshes
(@fig-consistency-curves). And the size of the baselines' dependence is
much larger on the cars than on the wings although the cars' cell-area
spread is the smaller (coefficient of variation 2.3 against 3.3), which
the cell-area spread alone does not explain and is an open question
(@sec-program-status).

### Where the slices sit: territories under a change of draw {#sec-territories}

**GeoTransolver's slices follow the points and ISLA's nearly do not: under
the 10:1-biased draw GeoTransolver's slice territories lose a third of
their agreement with the uniform draw beyond what a fresh uniform draw
costs, and its slice centroids move by 0.6 of the body's radius; ISLA loses
0.06 and its anchors move by 0.04.** The mechanism above was argued from
the equations; the probe here looks at the routing of the two
uniform-trained 100,000-cell checkpoints (ISLA at width 192, GeoTransolver
at width 256, both from @sec-equal-budget) on four validation cars under
three independent draws of the same surface: two uniform draws and the
10:1-biased draw of @fig-sampling-laws. For every
token the probe records its **dominant slice** in each block (the slice
with the largest read-back weight for ISLA, the largest slice weight for
GeoTransolver, head 0 shown), matches every token of one draw to its
nearest token of another on the surface, and counts how often the dominant
slice agrees. Two uniform draws set the **resampling floor**: soft
boundaries move a little under any resampling, so the floor is below one.
The **bias excess** is how much further the agreement falls when the
second draw is the biased one, and it is the quantity that separates the
two models.

```{python}
#| label: fig-territory-maps
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Slice territories of one validation car at block 6, one half of the
#|   body seen from the side, each point colored by its dominant slice (256
#|   slices, colors repeat). Top row ISLA, bottom row GeoTransolver; left
#|   column the uniform draw, right column the 10:1-biased draw of the same
#|   surface (denser toward the front). How to read this: colors are slice
#|   identities within one model and are not comparable between rows; a
#|   territory that keeps its place and its outline between the two columns is
#|   a function of the surface, one that moves is a function of the sample.
#|   The agreement printed in each right-hand panel is the fraction of its
#|   points whose slice equals that of the nearest uniform-draw point. Data:
#|   results/territory_pictures_2026-09-21.npz.
#| code-fold: true
T = np.load(RES / "territory_pictures_2026-09-21.npz")
cmap = plt.get_cmap("tab20")
fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10.0, 5.6), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for i, (name, label) in enumerate((("isla", STYLE["isla_ref"]["label"]), ("gt", STYLE["gt"]["label"]))):
    for j, draw in enumerate(("unif", "biased")):
        ax = axs[i, j]; p = T[f"{name}_{draw}_points"]; d = T[f"{name}_{draw}_dominant"].astype(int)
        m = p[:, 1] > 0                                  # one half of the car
        ax.scatter(p[m, 0], p[m, 2], c=cmap(d[m] % 20), s=1.2, linewidths=0, rasterized=True)
        ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.grid(False)
        ax.set_title(f"{label}, {'uniform draw' if draw == 'unif' else '10:1-biased draw'}", fontsize=9.5, loc="left")
        if draw == "biased":
            ax.text(0.98, 0.04, f"agreement with the uniform draw {float(T[f'{name}_agreement_block']):.2f}", transform=ax.transAxes, ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=9, path_effects=halo())
for ax in axs[-1]: ax.set_xlabel("x [m]")
for ax in axs[:, 0]: ax.set_ylabel("z [m]")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-territory-agreement
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Territory agreement per block for the two models. Filled markers: the
#|   resampling floor, the agreement between two independent uniform draws.
#|   Open markers: the agreement between the uniform draw and the 10:1-biased
#|   draw. The vertical distance between the two is the bias excess. How to
#|   read this: the floor is below one for both models because soft
#|   boundaries move under any resampling; what matters is whether the biased
#|   draw costs more agreement than a fresh uniform draw does. Four validation

for key, name in (("isla_ref", "ISLA"), ("gt", "GeoTransolver")):
    kw = series_kwargs(key); pb = R[name]["per_block"]; x = [r["block"] for r in pb]
    ax.plot(x, [r["floor"] for r in pb], marker=kw["marker"], color=kw["color"], ls="-", lw=1.4, ms=6, label=f"{STYLE[key]['label']}: two uniform draws (floor)")
    ax.plot(x, [r["agreement_biased"] for r in pb], marker=kw["marker"], color=kw["color"], mfc="white", mew=1.6, ls="--", lw=1.2, ms=6, label=f"{STYLE[key]['label']}: uniform against 10:1-biased")
```

```{python}
#| label: para-territory
#| output: asis
I, G = R["ISLA"]["summary"], R["GeoTransolver"]["summary"]
print(f"In median over the twelve blocks, ISLA's agreement between two uniform draws is {I['floor_median']:.2f} and between the uniform and the biased draw {I['agreement_biased_median']:.2f}, "
      f"a bias excess of {I['excess_median']:+.2f}; GeoTransolver's floor is {G['floor_median']:.2f} and its biased agreement {G['agreement_biased_median']:.2f}, an excess of {G['excess_median']:+.2f}. "
      f"The anchors move accordingly: the RMS displacement of ISLA's slice anchors between the two draws is {I['displacement_median']:.3f} of the body's RMS radius in median over blocks, "

```

Two qualifications. ISLA's territories are *nearly*, not exactly,
functions of the surface: the excess of 0.06 is just past the 0.05 the
probe preregistered as "unchanged", it is carried by the deep blocks (0.08
to 0.09 in blocks 8 to 11 against 0.03 to 0.06 in the first six), and
the anchors' 0.04 radii of motion is twice the 0.02 preregistered; the
likely source is the quadrature noise of a draw whose weights span a
decade, the same source the book gives for ISLA's 1.07x error growth under
this draw. On the wings (35-case rung, 200,000 cells) the anchor picture reproduces,
GeoTransolver's centroids moving 0.31 body radii and ISLA's anchors 0.004,
while the dominant-slice agreement no longer separates the models because
both wing checkpoints route softly (GeoTransolver's deep blocks are nearly
uniform over slices), so the agreement result is single-dataset and the
displacement result two-dataset (@sec-nb-territory-wings).

## Pose: a contract, not an accuracy edge {#sec-pose-contract}

```{python}
#| label: setup-pose

PA, PV, PN = POSE["arms"], POSE["verdict"], POSE["native_frame_reference"]
```

```{python}
#| label: para-pose
#| output: asis
print(f"**ISLA is exactly covariant to rotations and translations. When geometries arrive in arbitrary poses that exactness is worth "
      f"{(PV['gt_aug_posed_over_isla_posed']-1)*100:.0f}% against GeoTransolver and {(PV['t_aug_posed_over_isla_posed']-1)*100:.0f}% against "
      "Transolver trained with rotation augmentation, at the reporting protocol; when every case is in a native pose, or a canonical "
      "frame can be computed, it is a contract and not an accuracy edge.** Budget: 200,000 cells per case, 435 DrivAerML cars, float32, "
      f"two seeds. With every validation case in its own random pose, ISLA trained without augmentation scores {PA['isla']['posed_mean']:.4f} "
      f"(seeds {pseeds('isla')}), {PA['isla']['posed_over_native']:.3f}x its native-frame {PN['isla']:.4f}. GeoTransolver trained with rotation "
      f"augmentation scores {PA['gt_unit']['posed_mean']:.4f} ({PA['gt_unit']['posed_over_native']:.2f}x its native-pose {PN['gt_unit']:.4f}) and "
      f"Transolver with augmentation {PA['transolver_unit']['posed_mean']:.4f} ({PA['transolver_unit']['posed_over_native']:.2f}x its {PN['transolver_unit']:.4f}); "
      f"augmented baseline ÷ posed ISLA is {PV['gt_aug_posed_over_isla_posed']:.2f} and {PV['t_aug_posed_over_isla_posed']:.2f} "
      "(@sec-nb-p200k-pose-verdict). Data: results/p200k_pose_reduction_2026-09-19.json (native-frame references from "
      "results/p200k_trio_reduction_2026-09-19.json).")
```

```{python}
#| label: para-pose-canonical
#| output: asis
print("GeoTransolver trained in a canonical frame (freestream to +x, roll fixed from the geometry's principal axes; @sec-pose) is exactly "
      "pose-invariant at about a percent of in-distribution accuracy. What ISLA's construction still buys is generality: it needs no known global direction to "
      "canonicalize against and no sign-resolvable principal frame. Where those fail, on a geometry with a degenerate inertia tensor or in "
      "a setting without a global flow direction, the canonicalized model has no frame to compute, the augmented model pays the "
      f"{(PA['gt_unit']['posed_over_native']-1)*100:.0f} to {(PA['transolver_unit']['posed_over_native']-1)*100:.0f}% above, and the equivariant "
      "one is unaffected.")
```

ISLA's covariance is exact by
algebraic construction and verified to roundoff in float64; on the trained
GPU path it holds to 3e-5 in float32 and to about 4% under bf16 autocast,
so the contract is exercised at deployment only under float32 inference
(@sec-isla-contracts).

## Query independence and its price {#sec-query-independence}

**As shipped, ISLA's prediction at a surface point depends weakly on which
other points were sampled with it, more than GeoTransolver's does; the
optional passive decoder (@sec-isla-passive) removes that dependence
exactly, at a cost in accuracy that is a multiple rather than a
percentage.** Both sizes are being measured at the reporting protocol and
are not quoted here; the interior task shows the same trade, and its model
is deployed at its training query count (@sec-interior-companion).

## The frontier in one table {#sec-review-frontier}

**Every accuracy number in this chapter sits beside the same checkpoint's
behavior when the sampling or the pose changes, and beside its cost.**
Budget: the in-family column is the reporting protocol of 200,000 cells,
the density column the scaling budget of 100,000 (@sec-robustness-density),
the pose column the reporting protocol (@sec-pose-contract); the cost
frontier at 100,000 to 200,000 cells is @sec-equal-budget.
@tbl-consistency-matrix is the float32 standing of the three released
architectures, accuracy beside consistency. The frontier is stated as a
matrix, not a column (@sec-principle). On cost: at the reporting protocol
ISLA trains in 27 GB against GeoTransolver's 80 GB per device at 2.7x the
GPU-floor step time (@tbl-isla-cost); the fused geometry kernel, the
default on CUDA, and every other execution path compute the same function,
so no accuracy number in this chapter depends on the kernel
(@sec-isla-cost). The accuracy-against-memory frontier at 435 cars is
@fig-equal-budget in @sec-shared-floor.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-consistency-matrix
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
PP = json.load(open(RES / "p200k_pose_reduction_2026-09-19.json"))["arms"]
out = ("| configuration | in-family error (200,000 cells) | density 10:1 (x, 100,000 cells) | pose, random SO(3) (x, 200,000 cells) |\n|---|---:|---:|---:|\n")
for lab, arm, m, pk, note in (("ISLA", "isla", "isla", "isla", ""), ("GeoTransolver", "gt_unit_lr3e3", "gt_unit", "gt_unit", " (augmented)"),
                              ("Transolver", "transolver_unit_lr3e3", "transolver_unit", "transolver_unit", " (augmented)")):
    u = TDR[f"{m}_uniform"]["mean"]
    out += f"| {lab} | {TRIO[arm]['pressure_mean']:.4f} | {u['biased']/u['unif']:.1f} | {PP[pk]['posed_over_native']:.2f}{note} |\n"
print(out)
print(": Accuracy beside consistency on DrivAerML at full data, float32, unit-direction inputs for every architecture, each at its own best learning rate. "
      "In-family: surface-pressure error on 48 validation cars at the reporting protocol of 200,000 cells (@sec-full-data-accuracy). Density: error under 10:1 biased sampling with exact "
      "measure weights over the same model's error under uniform sampling, sample frame, on the uniform-trained checkpoints at 100,000 cells (@sec-robustness-density). Pose: error with every case in an arbitrary "
      "pose over the architecture's native-frame error at 200,000 cells; baselines trained with rotation augmentation, ISLA without (@sec-pose-contract). "
      "How to read this: each column is one instrument and one budget, so the columns are not comparable with one another; it does not show the wings, the ablations, or transfer to another vehicle family. Data: "
      "results/p200k_trio_reduction_2026-09-19.json; results/trainarea_dr_reduction_2026-09-20.json; results/p200k_pose_reduction_2026-09-19.json. {#tbl-consistency-matrix}")
```

The matrix splits the story in two. Accuracy: GeoTransolver + ISLA's
measure-weighted pooling (ablation) does not move the in-distribution
standing outside seed noise, so the measure is not what separates the
architectures in distribution. Consistency: the pooling repair does not
touch the frame, and with the center taken from the biased sample the
weighted baselines degrade by the same factors as the released ones; only
frames that read no biased statistic survive (@sec-robustness-density).
The baselines are the ones compared and are not modified.

## The capacity floor {#sec-shared-floor}

**At 435 DrivAerML cars both architectures reach the same accuracy floor,
about 0.040 in surface pressure, and ISLA reaches it cheaper: at matched
parameters of about 140M the two are identical (0.0406 each), ISLA comes
within 1% of the floor at half GeoTransolver's parameters, and on the
accuracy-against-memory frontier ISLA at 384 wide and 100,000 cells
(0.0411, 22 GB) matches GeoTransolver at 512 wide and 200,000 cells
(0.0410), which needs 4.5x the memory and 3.7x the GPU-floor step time.**
Budget: the scaling budget of 100,000 cells per case, where cells have
stopped paying for every model (@tbl-cells-ladder), so what remains is
capacity. @tbl-floor collects the lanes at the floor; the rest of the
section shows where they come from.

Three studies feed it. A cost grid varies cells per case and width at 435
DrivAerML cars (ISLA at widths 192 to 768 and 100,000 to 600,000 cells,
GeoTransolver at 256 and 512 wide and 100,000 to 400,000 cells, Transolver
at 256). A width and depth ladder at 100,000 cells takes ISLA to 1,536 wide
and 48 layers and GeoTransolver to 1,024 wide and 24 layers, with a
two-rate control on every rung. A routing study repeats the ISLA ladders
with the bounded cosine form of the routing softmax (@sec-isla-routing-forms)
in place of the linear form and adds GeoTransolver at 2,048 wide. Every lane
trains for 500 epochs with two seeds and is scored on the one instrument,
float32 at 200,000 cells, whatever count it trained at (the protocol is
converged: 1,000 epochs move neither model, @tbl-equal-budget). Every lane's
peak memory and step time are read from its own training log; the step
time is reported two ways, because at these sizes the median step is set
by the input pipeline (one case per GPU step) rather than by the network:
the tenth percentile of the logged steps is the *GPU-floor step time*, the
cost of the network alone; the median is the wall clock a user waits.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-floor
#| output: asis
ISO = J("isocost_reduction_2026-09-20.json")["configurations"]
CAPI = J("cap435_interim_2026-09-20.json")["configurations"]
EXT = J("routenorm_extension_2026-09-21.json")["configurations"]
# (architecture, routing, width x layers, training cells, displayed rate, source record)
floor_rows = [
    ("ISLA", "linear", "384 × 12", "100,000", "5e-4", ISO["isla|w384|c100k|lr5e-4|ep500"]),
    ("ISLA", "cosine", "384 × 24", "100,000", "5e-4", EXT["isla|cos|w384|d24|lr5e-4"]),
    ("ISLA", "cosine", "384 × 48", "100,000", "2.5e-4", EXT["isla|cos|w384|d48|lr2.5e-4"]),
    ("GeoTransolver", "as released", "512 × 12", "200,000", "3e-3", ISO["gt_unit|w512|c200k|lr3e-3|ep500"]),
    ("GeoTransolver", "as released", "512 × 24", "100,000", "3e-3", CAPI["gt|w512|d24|s256|lr3e-3"]),
    ("GeoTransolver", "as released", "1,024 × 12", "100,000", "1e-3", CAPI["gt|w1024|d12|s256|lr1e3"]),
    ("GeoTransolver", "as released", "2,048 × 12", "100,000", "1e-3", EXT["gt|w2048|d12|lr1e-3"]),
]
out = "| architecture | routing | width × layers | parameters | training cells | learning rate | surface pressure error, mean (seeds) | peak memory [GB] |\n|---|---|---|--:|--:|--:|---|--:|\n"
for arch, routing, shape, cells, lr, c in floor_rows:
    params = f"{c['params']/1e6:.0f}M" + (" (estimated)" if c.get("params_estimated") else "")
    seeds = " / ".join(f"{v:.4f}" for v in c["pressure_l2_seeds"])
    memv = c.get("peak_mem_gb")
    out += f"| {arch} | {routing} | {shape} | {params} | {cells} | {lr} | **{c['pressure_l2_mean']:.4f}** ({seeds}) | {'not logged' if memv is None else f'{memv:.0f}'} |\n"
print(out)
print(": The lanes of either architecture at or near the floor on DrivAerML: 435 training cars, 100,000 training cells "
      "per case (the scaling budget) except the 200,000-cell GeoTransolver row, all scored in float32 at 200,000 cells "
      "on the 48 validation cars, single dataset, 500 epochs, two seeds. *Parameters*: trainable, as counted by the "
      "training script; GeoTransolver-2,048's is extrapolated from its measured 256 to 1,024 ladder. *Peak memory*: "
      "peak of the logged per-step values on one GB300; not logged for the routing-study lanes. How to read this: the "
      "table names the floor and what each model pays to reach it, not a ranking (the errors differ by less than a "
      "seed spread); the cosine rows are ISLA's default candidate, not its shipped default. Data: "
      "results/isocost_reduction_2026-09-20.json, results/cap435_interim_2026-09-20.json, "
      "results/routenorm_extension_2026-09-21.json. {#tbl-floor}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-equal-budget
#| fig-cap: "Error against training cost for every scored lane of the cost grid and the width and depth ladders (435 DrivAerML cars, 500 epochs, two-seed means; trained at 100,000 to 600,000 cells per case as labeled, every lane scored in float32 at 200,000 cells). Top: peak GPU memory per device; bottom: GPU-floor step time (tenth percentile of the logged steps). Each marker is one configuration, labeled width x training cells (L24 for the 24-layer GeoTransolver); the step lines are each model's frontier, the best error attainable at or under a budget; GeoTransolver's recipe default (256 wide, 200,000 cells) is ringed. How to read this: below about 70 GB and 0.3 s the ISLA frontier lies under GeoTransolver's at every budget; above it GeoTransolver-1,024 and GeoTransolver-512 with 24 layers sit 1.2% below ISLA's best lane here. It does not show ISLA's depth ladder, which reaches the same floor (@fig-capacity) but whose cost was not logged in the same way. Data: results/isocost_reduction_2026-09-20.json and results/cap435_interim_2026-09-20.json."
#| fig-alt: "Two stacked scatter plots of validation pressure error against training cost, one against peak memory and one against GPU-floor step time, with ISLA points in blue, GeoTransolver in red and Transolver in amber, each with a step-shaped frontier line."
R = J("isocost_reduction_2026-09-20.json")
cfgs = [c for c in R["configurations"].values() if c["status"] == "complete" and c["epochs"] == 500 and c.get("peak_mem_gb") and c.get("step_s_p10")]
# the width and depth ladders add the wider and deeper lanes at 100,000 cells (default slice count; the rule learning rate for ISLA, the better rate for GeoTransolver)
CAP = J("cap435_interim_2026-09-20.json")
MODEL_KEY = {"isla": "isla", "gt": "gt_unit", "transolver": "transolver_unit"}
for c in CAP["configurations"].values():
    if c["status"] != "complete" or c.get("source") == "ISO-COST" or c["slices"] != 256 or not c.get("peak_mem_gb") or c["pressure_l2_mean"] > 0.1:
        continue
    cfgs.append(dict(model=MODEL_KEY[c["model"]], width=c["width"], cells=100000, epochs=500, lr=c["lr"], params=c["params"], depth=c["depth"],
                     pressure_l2_mean=c["pressure_l2_mean"], pressure_l2_seeds=c["pressure_l2_seeds"], peak_mem_gb=c["peak_mem_gb"],
                     step_s_p10=c["step_s_p10"], step_s_median=c["step_s_median"], status="complete"))
# GeoTransolver-512 keeps its better rate per configuration (prereg)
best = {}
for c in cfgs:
    k = (c["model"], c["width"], c["cells"], c.get("depth", 12 if c["model"] != "transolver_unit" else 8))
    if k not in best or c["pressure_l2_mean"] < best[k]["pressure_l2_mean"]:
        best[k] = c
cfgs = list(best.values())
KEY = {"isla": "isla_ref", "gt_unit": "gt", "transolver_unit": "t"}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(7.2, 7.6), sharey=True)
for ax, axis, xlabel in ((axes[0], "peak_mem_gb", "Peak GPU memory per device [GB]"), (axes[1], "step_s_p10", "GPU-floor step time, p10 [s]")):
    for model in ("isla", "gt_unit", "transolver_unit"):
        pts = sorted([c for c in cfgs if c["model"] == model], key=lambda c: c[axis])
        if not pts:
            continue
        kw = series_kwargs(KEY[model], ls="none")
        ax.plot([c[axis] for c in pts], [c["pressure_l2_mean"] for c in pts], **kw)
        # frontier: best error at or under each budget
        fx, fy, run = [], [], float("inf")
        for c in pts:
            run = min(run, c["pressure_l2_mean"]); fx.append(c[axis]); fy.append(run)
        ax.step(fx, fy, where="post", color=STYLE[KEY[model]]["color"], lw=1.6, alpha=0.55, label="_nolegend_")
        for c in pts:
            dep = c.get("depth", 12 if model != "transolver_unit" else 8)
            lab = f"{c['width']}x{c['cells']//1000}k" + ("" if dep in (8, 12) else f" L{dep}")
            ax.annotate(lab, (c[axis], c["pressure_l2_mean"]), textcoords="offset points",
                        xytext=(5, 4), fontsize=7.5, color=STYLE[KEY[model]]["color"],
                        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.1", fc=WHITE, ec="none", alpha=0.75))
    d = best.get(("gt_unit", 256, 200000, 12))
    if d:
        ax.plot([d[axis]], [d["pressure_l2_mean"]], marker="o", ms=15, mfc="none", mec=RED, mew=1.4, ls="none")
    ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel(xlabel); ax.grid(True, which="both", color=GRID, lw=0.6)
    ax.set_ylabel("surface-pressure error,\narea-weighted relative L2 [–]")
axes[0].legend(loc="upper right", frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-equal-budget
#| output: asis
rows = sorted(cfgs, key=lambda c: (c["model"] != "isla", c["model"], c["params"], c["cells"]))
NAME = {"isla": "ISLA", "gt_unit": "GeoTransolver", "transolver_unit": "Transolver"}
out = "| model | width (parameters) | cells per case | pressure L2, seeds | mean | peak memory [GB] | step p10 / median [s] |\n|---|---|--:|---|--:|--:|---|\n"
for c in rows:
    seeds = " / ".join(f"{v:.4f}" for v in c["pressure_l2_seeds"])
    lr_s = c["lr"] if "e-" in c["lr"] else c["lr"].replace("e", "e-")  # the ladder keys write 1e-3 as "1e3"
    lr = f", {lr_s}" if c["model"] == "gt_unit" and c["width"] >= 512 else ""
    dep = c.get("depth", 12 if c["model"] != "transolver_unit" else 8)
    dep_s = "" if dep in (8, 12) else f", {dep} layers"
    out += (f"| {NAME[c['model']]} | {c['width']} ({c['params']/1e6:.1f}M){lr}{dep_s} | {c['cells']//1000}k | {seeds} | **{c['pressure_l2_mean']:.4f}** | "
            f"{c['peak_mem_gb']:.0f} | {c['step_s_p10']:.2f} / {c['step_s_median']:.2f} |\n")
print(out)
print(": Every scored configuration of the cost grid and the width and depth ladders at the default slice count "
      "(435 DrivAerML cars, 500 epochs, two seeds; training cells per case as listed, every row scored in float32 at "
      "200,000 cells on the 48 validation cars). GeoTransolver is at its better learning rate per configuration; its "
      "256-wide 200,000-cell row is the reporting-protocol pair at 3e-3 with the step time of the same configuration's "
      "1,000-epoch control. Costs are per-lane medians over the run (memory: peak of the logged per-step values) on "
      "one GB300. How to read this: rows differ in width, parameters and cells at once, so a comparison across "
      "architectures must be read at matched memory or matched parameters (@tbl-floor), not down the column. "
      "Data: results/isocost_reduction_2026-09-20.json and results/cap435_interim_2026-09-20.json. {#tbl-equal-budget}")
```

Four readings carry the section.

1. **Cells per case stop paying at 100,000.** Down every column of
   @tbl-cells-ladder the error moves by less than a seed spread from 100,000
   to 600,000 cells: ISLA-192 spans 0.0448 to 0.0452, GeoTransolver-256
   0.0445 to 0.0447, and a joint fit
   $\varepsilon = a N^{-\alpha} + b P^{-\beta} + c$ in training cells $N$
   and parameters $P$ returns $\alpha = 0.00 \pm 0.02$ for ISLA. The
   count-noise mechanism that bought ISLA 19% from 10,000 to 200,000 cells
   (@sec-scoreboard-200k) is spent by 100,000, and the training budget is
   not what limits either model: 1,000 epochs instead of 500 move ISLA-192
   and GeoTransolver-256 at 200,000 cells by 0.03% each.
2. **Width pays, for both, up to about 35M parameters.** ISLA-384 improves
   on ISLA-192 by 8.7% at 100,000 cells and 7.1% at 200,000;
   GeoTransolver-512 improves on GeoTransolver-256 by 6.7% at 100,000 and
   7.9% at 200,000 (@tbl-equal-budget). Above that ISLA's width curve turns
   over (0.0426 at 512, 0.0421 at 768, 0.0429 at 1,024, 0.0452 at 1,536
   under linear routing), and the turnover is a property of the width axis
   and not of the width learning-rate rule (@sec-using-lr): the rate
   controls found the rule rate to be the best clean rate at every width,
   and removing the ceiling with cosine routing leaves the ladder flat from
   384 to 768 and declining after.
3. **At equal cost ISLA is ahead up to about 70 GB.** ISLA-384 at 100,000
   cells (0.0411, 22 GB, 0.12 s GPU floor) is the best lane of either model
   below 70 GB and 0.3 s per step; above that budget GeoTransolver's best
   lanes (0.0406 at 74 GB and at 96 GB) are 1.2% lower than any ISLA lane on
   the cost grid, and level with ISLA's depth ladder at about 140M
   parameters (reading 4).
4. **Both architectures reach the same floor, about 0.040, and ISLA reaches
   it with fewer parameters along its depth axis.** @fig-capacity puts every
   ladder on one axis of parameter count. GeoTransolver's width ladder
   improves by 6.7%, 2.6% and 0.7% per doubling from 256 to 2,048 wide and
   ends at 0.0403 with about 571M parameters; the last doubling buys the
   size of a seed spread. ISLA's width ladder turns over above 768
   whichever routing form is used, so width is not ISLA's axis past 35M
   parameters. Its depth axis is: under cosine routing, which removes the
   learning-rate ceiling that made the linear 48-layer model untrainable
   (@sec-robustness-lr), 384 wide with 24 layers reads 0.0407 at 68M
   parameters and 48 layers 0.0406 at 136M (@tbl-floor). At matched
   parameters of about 140M the two architectures are identical
   (0.0406 against GeoTransolver-1,024's 0.0406); ISLA comes within 1% of
   the floor at half GeoTransolver's parameters (68M against 143M) and at
   about half of GeoTransolver-1,024's training memory (42 against 74 GB).
   Data: results/cap435_reduction_2026-09-20.json,
   results/routenorm_interim_2026-09-20.json,
   results/routenorm_extension_2026-09-21.json.

```{python}
#| label: fig-capacity
#| fig-cap: >

#|   Red: GeoTransolver's width ladder (filled) and its 24-layer lane at 512

#|   wide under cosine routing (open diamonds, dotted). The gray band is the
#|   floor both architectures reach, 0.040 to 0.041. How to read this: the

#|   results/cap435_reduction_2026-09-20.json,
#|   results/routenorm_interim_2026-09-20.json,

#| code-fold: true
CFG = J("cap435_reduction_2026-09-20.json")["configurations"]
RNC = J("routenorm_interim_2026-09-20.json")["configurations"]
EXT = J("routenorm_extension_2026-09-21.json")["configurations"]
def cap_pt(k): c = CFG[k]; return c["params"], c["pressure_l2_mean"], c["pressure_l2_seeds"]
def rn_pt(k, params): c = RNC[k]; return params, c["mean"], c["seeds"]
def ext_pt(k): c = EXT[k]; return c["params"], c["pressure_l2_mean"], c["pressure_l2_seeds"]
PW = {w: CFG[f"isla|w{w}|d12|s256|lr{lr}"]["params"] for w, lr in ((192, "1e-3"), (384, "5e-4"), (768, "2.5e-4"))}
gt_w = [cap_pt("gt|w256|d12|s256|lr3e-3"), cap_pt("gt|w512|d12|s256|lr3e-3"), cap_pt("gt|w1024|d12|s256|lr1e3"), ext_pt("gt|w2048|d12|lr1e-3")]
gt_d = [cap_pt("gt|w512|d12|s256|lr3e-3"), cap_pt("gt|w512|d24|s256|lr3e-3")]
isla_lin = [cap_pt("isla|w192|d12|s256|lr1e-3"), cap_pt("isla|w384|d12|s256|lr5e-4"), cap_pt("isla|w512|d12|s256|lr3.75e-4"),
            cap_pt("isla|w768|d12|s256|lr2.5e-4"), cap_pt("isla|w1024|d12|s256|lr1.875e-4"), cap_pt("isla|w1536|d12|s256|lr1.25e-4")]
isla_cos = [rn_pt("cars|cos|w192|lr1e-3", PW[192]), rn_pt("cars|cos|w384|lr5e-4", PW[384]), rn_pt("cars|cos|w768|lr5e-4", PW[768]),
            ext_pt("isla|cos|w1024|d12|lr5e-4"), ext_pt("isla|cos|w1536|d12|lr5e-4")]
isla_dep = [rn_pt("cars|cos|w384|lr5e-4", PW[384]), ext_pt("isla|cos|w384|d24|lr5e-4"), ext_pt("isla|cos|w384|d48|lr2.5e-4")]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.6, 5.2))
def draw(series, key, label, ls="-", marker=None, mfc=None):
    kw = series_kwargs(key, lw=1.8, ms=7); kw["ls"] = ls
    if marker: kw["marker"] = marker
    if mfc is not None: kw["mfc"] = mfc
    ax.plot([s[0] for s in series], [s[1] for s in series], label=label, **{k: v for k, v in kw.items() if k != "label"}, zorder=3)
    for x, _, seeds in series:
        ax.plot([x] * len(seeds), seeds, ls="none", marker="_", color=kw["color"], ms=8, mew=1.1, zorder=4)
draw(gt_w, "gt", "GeoTransolver, width 256 → 2,048 (12 layers)")
draw(gt_d, "gt", "GeoTransolver, 512 wide, 12 → 24 layers", ls=":", mfc="white")
draw(isla_lin, "isla_ref", "ISLA, linear routing, width 192 → 1,536 (12 layers; width-rule rate)", ls="--", mfc="white")
draw(isla_cos, "isla_ref", "ISLA, cosine routing, width 192 → 1,536 (12 layers; best clean rate)")
draw(isla_dep, "isla_ref", "ISLA, cosine routing, 384 wide, 12 → 48 layers", ls=":", marker="D", mfc="white")
ax.axhspan(0.0399, 0.0411, color=GRID, zorder=0)
ax.text(6.5e6, 0.0405, "the floor: 0.040 to 0.041", fontsize=8.5, color=INK2, va="center", path_effects=halo())
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlim(5e6, 1.0e9); ax.set_ylim(0.039, 0.0485)
ax.set_xlabel("trainable parameters [count]"); ax.set_ylabel("surface-pressure error,\narea-weighted relative L2 [–]")
ax.set_xticks([1e7, 3e7, 1e8, 3e8, 1e9]); ax.set_xticklabels(["10M", "30M", "100M", "300M", "1B"])
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8.2)
plt.show()
```

These are one dataset's numbers; the same grid on the 510-wing
HiLiftAeroML rung decides whether "width, not cells" and the shared floor
are properties of the architectures or of DrivAerML (@sec-program-status).

## Regime extrapolation: angle of attack and stall {#sec-regime-extrapolation}

**Trained on one flow regime, neither architecture predicts the other:
crossing from low to high angle of attack, or from attached to separated
flow, multiplies surface-pressure error by roughly ten, to a level worse
than any architecture reaches from only 35 training cases inside the
regime.** Budget: the exploration budget of 10,000 cells per case, two
seeds; the ISLA lanes on these splits are the legacy centered variant
(removed), and ISLA itself has not been trained on them, so the finding is
stated for the architectures and not as a comparison between them.
HiLiftAeroML ships two curated partitions along this axis: the **aoa
split** trains on 788 cases at 12° or less, validates on 112 further
low-angle cases and holds a sealed test set of all 900 cases at 14° or
more; the **stall split** trains on 942 pre-stall cases, validates on 135
and holds a sealed test set of 723 post-stall cases. The GeoTransolver
lanes consumed the physical freestream velocity (@sec-part-baseline), so
the table shows the within-architecture degradation ratio $d \equiv$
(seed-mean sealed-test error in the other regime) ÷ (seed-mean validation
error in the training regime) only; each sealed test was evaluated exactly
once under a protocol declared beforehand.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-hilift-ood
#| output: asis
lad = json.load(open(RES / "hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json"))
sealed = json.load(open(RES / "hilift_sealed_test_2026-09-04.json")); runs = sealed["runs"]
def d_of(arch, axis):
    ks = [f"lad_hl_{arch}_{axis}_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43)]
    return mean(runs[k]["pressure_l2"] for k in ks) / mean(lad[k]["pressure_l2"] for k in ks)
out = "| split (train → sealed test) | GeoTransolver, d | legacy centered variant (removed), d |\n|---|---:|---:|\n"
for axis, lab in (("aoa", "aoa (12° or less → 14° or more)"), ("stall", "stall (pre-stall → post-stall)")):
    out += f"| {lab} | {d_of('gt', axis):.1f} | {d_of('mt2', axis):.1f} |\n"
print(out)
print(": Regime extrapolation on HiLiftAeroML at the exploration budget (10,000 cells, two seeds): the degradation ratio d, seed-mean "
      "sealed-test error in the other regime over seed-mean in-regime validation error, for each trained configuration. How to read "
      "this: d is a within-configuration ratio; the two columns are not a comparison of the architectures' accuracy (the GeoTransolver "
      "lanes consumed the physical freestream velocity, and the second column is the removed variant, not ISLA). "
      "Data: results/hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json (validation), "
      "results/hilift_sealed_test_2026-09-04.json (test, with the sealed-test declaration recorded inside). {#tbl-hilift-ood}")
```

Both configurations lose a factor of about ten, from 0.021 to 0.030 in
regime to 0.24 to 0.33 on the sealed test; velocity and wall shear degrade
the same way. A model that has seen hundreds of cases of the wrong regime is
less useful than one that has seen 35 spanning both: coverage, not
architecture, governs this axis. GeoTransolver's smaller ratio is the
arithmetic of a higher in-regime floor, since the two converge to similar
sealed-test error from different starting points. In practice a regime
boundary must be covered by training data, a validation set drawn from the
training regime overstates the model's range by an order of magnitude, and
any reported accuracy for these surrogates should state the angle-of-attack
and flow-state coverage of the training data alongside the error.

### The smaller ratio is not carried by raw coordinates {#sec-ood-mechanism}

The one mechanism proposed for GeoTransolver's smaller ratio, that its raw
coordinates carry a learned map from position on the wing to pressure
across the regime boundary, was tested by adding a raw-coordinate channel
to the legacy centered variant on the stall split with preregistered bars
and one sealed-test evaluation per seed: the channel left in-regime
accuracy and sealed-test error where they were on both seeds
(results/b1_raw_coordinate_discriminator_2026-09-07.json), so the smaller
ratio is arithmetic and not a transfer mechanism its inputs carry.
